background.definition: Abruptio placentae (placental abruption) involves the premature separation of the normally implanted placenta, occurring after 20 weeks of gestation but prior to delivery. Placental abruption is one of the obstetric conditions that constitutes the syndrome of Ischemic Placental Disease.

list.listitem: Overall incidence ranges from 0.5% to 1% of births.
In a population-based study, placental abruption was recorded in 4.8 per 1000 primiparous singleton births and 5.9 per 1000 multiparous singleton births.

A nationwide population-based study using data from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway and Statistics Norway (1990-2016) showed immigrant women from sub-Saharan Africa, especially Ethiopia, have increased odds (1.35; 95% CI 1.15-1.58) for placental abruption when giving birth in Norway.
Affects 1% of pregnancies worldwide.

Based on a hospital database of 27,796,465 singleton births in the U.S. between 2006 and 2012, the prevalence rate of abruption was 9.6 per 1000; two-thirds of cases were classified as severe (6.5 per 1000).
Fifty percent of abruptions occur in pregnancies less than 36 weeks of gestation, resulting in high expenditures for the care of premature infants and associated complications of prematurity.
About 10% of preterm births, 10% to 20% of all perinatal deaths and significant maternal morbidity are caused by placental abruption.

Authors of a systemic review of 123 studies concluded that there are several adverse outcomes for mother and fetus. Adverse maternal outcomes included elevated risk of cesarean delivery, postpartum hemorrhage and transfusion, in addition to relaparotomy, hysterectomy, sepsis, amniotic fluid embolism, venous thromboembolism, acute kidney injury, and maternal intensive care unit admission

Based on this study, there is an increassed risk to the fetus of acidosis, encephalopathy, severe respiratory disorders, necrotizing enterocolitis, acute kidney injury, need for resuscitation, chronic lung disease, infant death, and epilepsy in surviving neonates.
The key risk factor for poor neonatal outcome among African American women with placental abruption is due to prematurity at delivery.
In a population based retrospective cohort study between 2001 to 2007, placental abruption was an indepedent risk factor for development of DIC in women with HELLP syndrome.
Prior term placental abruption increases the risk of preterm delivery in the subsequent pregnancies (RR 2.3, 95% CI 1.7-3.1).

Adverse perinatal outcomes such as early preterm delivery (35.3 vs 37.9 weeks) occur more frequently in recurrent placental abruption compared to first time abruption. The rates of umbilical artery pH <7.1 and 5-min Apgar score <7 were also significantly higher in the recurrence group (21% vs 13% and 20% vs 10%, respectively).
Placental abruption is a risk factor for heart failure, particularly in women who also had hypertensive disorder and preterm birth.

Abruption during pregnancy is associated with long-term maternal cardiovascular disease, and with increased rates of nonfatal ischemic stroke (HR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1-1.7) and hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1-1.9).

Based on data from the Finnish Registry observational study, a history of placental abruption was associated with an increased risk of lung cancer (SIR 1.51; 95% CI 1.05-2.10) and thyroid cancer (SIR 1.47; 95% CI 1.04-2.02).
Overall mortality (hazard ratio 8.70; 95% CI 6.96-10.90) among offspring of abruption extend beyond perinatal period due to birth related asphyxia and prematurity.

In a hospital-based cohort study over a 22-year period, investigators found abruption was associated with increased rates of cerebral palsy (hazard ratio [HR] 6.71; 95% CI 3.32, 13.58) and developmental disorders (HR 3.36, 95% CI 1.38, 8.13) in the offsprin later in life.
Maternal hypertension (most common cause of abruption) and other maternal vascular disease.
Trauma or rapid uterine decompression.
Uterine structural anomalies.
Maternal cocaine abuse.
Placental separation results from bleeding into the decidua basalis from damaged or ruptured small decidual arteries.
Pressure caused by hematoma formation further separates the placenta from the uterine wall.
Fetal compromise occurs as a result of compression and decreased blood supply.
Couvelaire uterus occurs when retroplacental blood traverses the uterus to reach the peritoneum. Weakening of the myometrium may result in uterine rupture with contractions.
Severity of fetal and maternal distress correlates with the degree of placental separation.
Complete abruption causes fetal death unless emergent delivery occurs.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Prior history of miscarriage (3 or more)
Advanced maternal age (>34 years controlling for hypertension)
Air pollution: PM2.5 and nitrogen dioxide ≥95th percentile
Air pollution: PM2.5 ≥95th percentile and nitrogen dioxide <95th percentile

list.listitem: Because of the association between hypertensive disorders and abruption, interventions involving management of hypertension can decrease the risk of abruption. A

The use of nifedipine and methyldopa for treatment of chronic hypertension are associated with significantly lower placental abruption rates (odds ratio 0.29 [95% CI 0.15-0.58] and 0.23 [95% CI 0.11-0.46] respectively).
Tobacco, cocaine, methamphetamine, and other illicit substances should be avoided during pregnancy. C

Vitamin C/E supplementation starting at 9 to 16 weeks in low-risk nulliparous women with singleton gestations reduced the risk of placental abruption in smokers (relative risk [RR] 0.09; 95% CI 0.00-0.87], but not in nonsmokers. Folic acid and other vitamin supplementation during pregnancy may reduce the risk of placental abruption based on one population-based study.

Aspirin use at 100 mg or more daily started before 16 weeks' gestation may reduce the risk of placental abruption (RR 0.62; 95% CI 0.31-1.26), but in this meta-analysis of 20 trials focused on prevention of preeclampsia, confidence intervals were wide likely due to the rare occurrence of abruption (1.3% of cases in this study).

Seatbelts should be correctly and consistently worn during all trimesters of pregnancy (3-point restraints with the upper belt worn between the breasts and the lower belt worn straight across the hips).C

In gravid women with preeclampsia, magnesium sulfate administration (4 g IV load followed by 1 g per hour for 24 hours) decreases the risk of placental abruption (2.0% vs 3.2%; 95% CI 0.3-2.1; NNT = 83).

There is controversy over whether antenatal antithrombotic therapy can prevent placental dysfunction in high-risk women. Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 small trials concluded that heparin treatment was associated with a reduction in the risk of pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and low birthweight; data on serious infant health outcomes was lacking.

In a small RCT with 110 high-risk women without thrombophilia, antenatal low-molecular weight heparin (Dalteparin) was associated with a reduction in the combined outcome of severe pre-eclampsia, low birth weight, or major abruptio placentae (5.5% [n = 3/55] vs 23.6% [n = 13/55]).

However, investigators failed to find a reduced risk of recurrent placenta-mediated pregnancy complications in at-risk women using low-molecular-weight heparin based on data from 963 women from 8 RCTs.
Vaginal bleeding (70%), abdominal pain (51%), blood-tinged amniotic fluid (50%), and fetal heart rate abnormalities (69%) are the most common manifestations. B
Assess the patient clinically for abruption severity and need for emergent delivery. C
Ultrasound plays a limited role in diagnosing abruption. B
Definitive management should never be delayed for ultrasound evaluation because it does not reliably diagnose abruption. B

No significant pain between contractions; uterus relaxed between contractions

Elevated white blood cell count; right-sided abdominal pain which localizes; anorexia

list.listitem: Abruption is classified by severity using the following system: Grade 0: Asymptomatic blood clot or indentation found on postpartum examination of the placenta. Grade 1: Vaginal bleeding and mild uterine tenderness are noted in absence of maternal or fetal distress (50% of abruptions). Grade 2: Vaginal bleeding ranging from moderate to none; uterine tenderness and moderate to tetanic contractions; maternal tachycardia and orthostatic changes; fetal distress; hypofibrinogenemia (about 30% of abruptions). Grade 3: Severe; vaginal bleeding ranging from none to severe; painful tetanic uterus; maternal shock and fetal death; coagulopathy (25% of cases).

Vaginal bleeding (70%), abdominal pain (51%), blood-tinged amniotic fluid (50%), and fetal heart rate abnormalities (69%) are the most common manifestations. Vaginal bleeding often occurs with placental abruption; however, 19% of women have neither bleeding nor pain.

Concealed abruption occurs because the expanding hematoma between the uterine wall and placenta does not reach the edge of the placenta. Revealed abruption occurs once the bleeding extends past the placental edge, creating a space between the chorion and decidua that tracks down to the cervix.
If bleeding traverses the placenta, blood-tinged amniotic fluid will be seen.
Pain over the uterus is a prominent characteristic; it typically occurs both during and between regular contractions.
The uterus is hard and tender, without relaxation between contractions, and palpating fetal parts is difficult.
Fetal heart tones are not heard in cases of fetal death.
Placental abruption is a clinical diagnosis. Diagnosis is confirmed by presence of a retroplacental clot or indentation of the placental surface noted after delivery.
However, the concordance between clinical and histologic diagnosis is poor.

Blood type and Rh; type and cross 2 units; CBC with platelet count; PT, PTT, INR; electrolytes for renal function; fibrin split products [not specific in pregnancy for diagnosing disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)].

C-reactive protein (CRP) is not clinically relevant in distinguishing between woman with and without placental abruption, although significantly increased CRP levels are found in women with abruption. There is no difference in CRP levels between bleeding and non-bleeding abruption.

In a systematic review of observational studies, low levels of pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) during the first trimester and a uterine artery pulsatility index >90th centile during the second trimester had a moderate to high predictive accuracy for stillbirth related to placental abruption, small-for-gestational-age or pre-eclampsia (positive LRs from 6.3-14.1 and negative LRs from 0.1-0.4). PAPP-A was also found to be associated with placental abruption after adjusting for presence of hypertension in a large population-based study (OR 1.9; 95% CI 1.2-3.1). An alpha fetoprotein at the 95th percentile or greater (OR 2.3; 95% CI 1.4-3.8) was also statistically significantly associated with abruption.

In a secondary analysis of data of 35,307 women (250 abruption cases) enrolled in the First and Second Trimester Evaluation of Risk cohort, an abnormally low PAPP-A (fifth percentile or less) increased risk of abruption (RR 1.9; 95% CI 1.2-2.8). In addition, maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein at the 95th percentile or greater and Inhibin-A at the 5th percentile or less increased abruption risk; the presence of all three markers increased the risk to 8.8-fold (95% CI 2.3-34.3).

Metabolomic profile of early pregnancy such as dodecanoylcarnitine/dodecenoylcarnitine (C12/C12:1), and phosphatidylcholine acyl-alkyl C 38:1 (PC ae C38:1) in addition to vaginal bleeding served as a marker for abruption risk in a small study.

One nulliparous woman out of 10 with first-trimester positive preterm preeclampsia screening test identified as high risk by the Fetal Medicine Foundation algorithm developed at least 1 severe placenta-mediated pregnancy complication.

Ultrasound plays a limited role in diagnosing abruption; it is only 24% sensitive. If the ultrasound is abnormal, abruption is likely (specificity 96%, PV+ 88%). Over time, clots become echo-free and allow for identification of abruption after the fact.

Definitive management should never be delayed for ultrasound evaluation, because it does not reliably diagnose abruption; with acute, severe abruption, acoustic characteristics of a fresh retroplacental clot mimic those of normal placenta, confusing the diagnosis.
In 1 small case series, CT scan was 42.9% sensitive and 89.7% specific for placental abruption following abdominal trauma.
Prediction models that combine risk factors (eg, maternal age >34 years, parity >3, current smoking) have poor sensitivity for determining abruption risk.

Take a thorough history of gestational age and symptoms (eg, vaginal bleeding, contractions, trauma, smoking or drug use) and perform a speculum exam to assess bleeding. Assess uterine tenderness and hemodynamic stability.
Order appropriate lab tests and use fetal monitoring to assess fetal wellbeing.

In severely preterm pregnancies with suspected mild abruption, delivery may be postponed to allow for administration of corticosteroids; any evidence of maternal or fetal compromise requires delivery. Consider use of corticosteroids in cases with mild abruption and gestational age less than 34 weeks.
In severe abruption (eg, nonreassuring fetal heart rate, evidence of maternal shock), emergent delivery via cesarean or operative vaginal delivery (if possible) should occur immediately.

In cases of clinically diagnosed abruption, severe placental abruption is correlated with poor neonatal outcomes and there was a significant correlation between the onset-to-delivery time and the umbilical artery pH in the moderate group (R = -0.43)
In suspected mild abruption that occurs in preterm pregnancy, watchful waiting is an option, with administration of corticosteroids to expedite fetal lung maturity. C

The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine recommends that in women with active hemorrhage in the late preterm period (34 0/7-36 6/7 weeks of gestation), delivery should not be delayed for the purpose of administering antenatal corticosteroids. B
Evidence of maternal (eg, hemodynamic instability, DIC) or fetal (eg, heart rate abnormalities) compromise necessitates immediate delivery. C
A decision-to-delivery interval of less than 20 minutes in cases of severe abruption may result in better outcomes for the fetus (case-control study). B
Tocolysis is generally contraindicated except in very mild abruptions prior to 34 weeks gestation; tocolysis may be considered in this case to allow time for administration of corticosteroids.
RCTs comparing management strategies for abruption are unavailable.
If the fetus is alive and the gestational age advanced enough that survival is probable, cesarean delivery should be performed.
A decision-to-delivery interval of 20 minutes or less improved fetal outcomes in a study of severe abruption.
If abruption occurs during the second stage of labor, operative vaginal delivery (ie, forceps or vacuum) can be attempted.
If the fetus is dead, delivery should be attempted vaginally.

In suspected abruption that occurs in preterm pregnancy and is mild, watchful waiting may be an option. Administration of corticosteroids to expedite fetal lung maturity is indicated. Evidence of maternal or fetal compromise necessitates immediate delivery.

The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine recommends that in women with active hemorrhage in the late preterm period (34 0/7-36 6/7 weeks of gestation), delivery should not be delayed for the purpose of administering antenatal corticosteroids.
Pregnant women with unexplained vaginal bleeding or contractions should be evaluated and triaged in an inpatient hospital setting.
A physician capable of performing an emergent cesarean delivery must be involved.
Contingency planning for postoperative management in an intensive care setting should be considered.
Major immediate maternal risk is hemorrhagic shock.

Ten percent of abruptions are associated with thromboplastin release into the maternal circulation; in these cases, diffuse intravascular coagulopathy is more likely, especially in cases of fetal death.
Acute tubular necrosis and cortical necrosis are seen in severe cases.
Management includes aggressive blood and fluid replacement in cases of severe hemorrhagic shock and replacement of clotting factors as needed.
An abnormal fetal heart rate, especially bradycardia, is a predictor of fetal acidemia (pH <7) and poor outcome.

Major congenital anomalies, including central nervous system, cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary and musculoskeletal anomalies, are about two-fold greater in pregnancies complicated by placental abruption (OR 1.9; 95% CI 1.6-2.5).
Prognosis improves with timely diagnosis and intervention.

Women with preeclampsia experiencing abruption have poorer maternal, fetal and neonatal outcomes. Concurrently presenting preeclampsia increases the odds of grade III abruption to 5.27 (95% CI 2.346, 12.41) compared to patients who did not have concurrent preeclampsia.

Risk of future abruption is directly related to prior history. If a woman has one previous abruption, the risk of future abruption increases to 10% to 17%. If a woman has a history of two previous abruptions, risk increases to over 20% in future pregnancies. C
The odds ratio for a subsequent pregnancy ending in stillbirth is increased for women who had a previous abruption (OR 2.8; 95% CI 2.2-3.5). B

Previous cesarean delivery increases risk for both placenta previa and abruption in future pregnancies. Risk of abruption in subsequent pregnancy was 30% higher after cesarean compared with vaginal delivery. B
Maternal death: In a population study in Finland, of 7735 placental abruptions identified there were three maternal deaths giving a case fatality rate of 0.4 per 1000 cases. B
Although maternal death is rare, maternal death following abruption is seven times higher than the overall maternal mortality rate.

Neonatal death: Abruption results in neonatal death in 10% to 30% of cases; most occur in utero. Adverse neonatal outcomes in fetuses that survive are due to complications of prematurity. Risk factors for placental abruption-related perinatal mortality are prematurity, low birthweight, male fetal sex and maternal smoking. B

Other subsequent risks: Women who have a history of placental abruption may also have more atherosclerotic risk factors than women without this history including higher blood pressures, poorer lipid values and higher fasting blood glucose. B
Children born to mothers with placental abruption compared to normal birth, did not show a significantly higher cumulative incidence of long-term cardiovascular morbidity (1.0% vs 0.6%).
